blocks.text: And Artemidorus, Onirocritica book 1, ch. 30: Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομένας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· [Pareias ischnas echein, ē helkomenas, lypas, ē penthos sēmainei. ischnas men lypas, helkomenas de penthos. kai gar en tois penthesi lōbōntai tas pareias hoi anthrōpoi] To have thin or ulcerated cheeks (in dreams) signifies sorrow and mourning: thin cheeks sorrow, ulcerated ones mourning. For in mourning people tear their cheeks. I admit that I have read in Horus, Hieroglyph. book 2, ch. 50, that the turtledove has teeth. To signify a nursing woman, and one who nourishes well, he says, (the Egyptians) τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει [trygona zōgraphousin; hautē gar monē tōn allōn ptēnōn odontas, kai masthous echei], paint a turtledove: for she alone among birds has teeth and breasts. If this were true, she would also have jaws and cheeks. But learned men have already observed that this belongs to the bat, to which alone it applies. So some change τρυγόνα [trygona] into τριγόνα [trigona], conjecturing that the bat is called by that name there, because τρίζειν [trizein, to squeak] is proper to it. Others more correctly change it into νυκτερίδα [nykterida]; and the reason why the words were interchanged is obvious. Immediately before it had said: Wishing to signify a weak man who attempts great things, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν [nykterida zōgraphousin], they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And immediately after follows: To designate a man who is charmed by dancing and the pipe, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν [trygona zōgraphousin], they paint a turtledove, which is caught by the pipe and dancing. I have rendered turtledove with Mercerus, Caussinus and others. Yet — and I am surprised this escaped them — τρυγὼν [trygōn] there is not the turtledove but the stingray, which this same writer below, in ch. 105, calls simply τρυγόνα [trygona], and others, to distinguish it, θαλαττίαν τρυγόνα [thalattian trygona], the sea turtledove. For it is not the bird, the turtledove, but ἡ θαλαττία τρυγὼν [hē thalattia trygōn], the sea turtledove, that is, the stingray, that, charmed by the pipe and dancing, is lured into the fish-trap, as Aelian relates at length, On Animals book 17, ch. 18; although Philo too refers this to the turtledove, the bird. Now, to return to where the discussion digressed: the words of the Sacred Song in Hebrew read thus: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Your cheeks are adorned with rows (of gems), your neck with chains. [II, 600] For this the Greeks have Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos, trachēlos sou hōs hormiskoi?] and Jerome: How beautiful have your cheeks become, like the turtledove's; your neck like a necklace. For, interchanging ב and כ, they read כתורים for בתורים, and כחרוזים for בחרוזים, and they took תורי for turtledoves, whereas there it means rows, namely of gems, or of golden studs. That it must be rendered so is shown by many things: 1. תורים and חרוזים are here nearly synonymous. Moreover, although the word חרוזים does not occur elsewhere in Scripture, it is very well known from the Arabic language, in which the verb خرز [kharaza] means to sew with an awl, and الخرز [al-kharaz] a necklace of gems strung together, and also the spine, whose vertebrae are as it were sewn and strung together. Accordingly the Greek renders חרוזים as ὁρμισκοὺς [hormiskous], and Jerome as necklaces, entirely correctly. 2. Immediately there follows תורי זהב נעשה לך, where it is plain that תורי are not turtledoves but a kind of golden ornament, namely chains or something similar. Hence there Jerome has: We will make you golden chains. And the Syriac ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ, a golden chain. And the fifth edition στρεπτὸν χρυσίου [strepton chrysiou]; so it should be read, not στρεπτοῦ [streptou]. For στρεπτὸς [streptos] or στρεπτὸν [strepton] is used everywhere for a torque by Herodotus, Xenophon, Plutarch and others. In Symmachus, for περίβλεπτα χρυσίου [periblepta chrysiou] I would read περίπλεκτα [periplekta]. For στρέφειν [strephein], whence στρεπτὸν [strepton], and πλέκειν [plekein], whence πλεκτὸν [plekton], are nearly synonymous. Hence in Hesychius πλόκιον [plokion] is εἶδος περιδεραίου [eidos perideraiou], a kind of necklace. And the same reasoning holds for the Syriac ܥܢܩܐ for torque, for the verb ܥܢܩ means to fold and to twist. But why do the Elders render ὁμοιώματα [homoiōmata]? Did they read ציורי, that is, images, for תורי? Or did they think that תורי זהב meant likenesses of turtledoves made of gold, which was the opinion of Aben Ezra? 3. Indeed, תור with Thau here is the same as טור with Teth, a word Moses uses repeatedly for a row of gems, as in Exod. XXVIII, 17: ארבעה טורים אבן, four rows of stones. Likewise, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, sardius, topaz and emerald, the first row. 5. Nor is it obscure how cheeks are adorned with rows of gems: namely if these hang from the ears, or if they are scattered over the ribbons of the mitres, that is, the broad bands that were drawn down along the cheeks and tied under the chin. For in Syria the mitre was a woman's head-covering. Virgil in the Catalecta: [col. 58]
The Syrian tavern-hostess, her head bound with a Greek little mitre.
Go, you who fancy a barbarian harlot with a painted mitre.
Barbarian, that is, Syrian; for there had preceded:
